_comment: Intentional differences between the sidecar's baked registry and app/core/registry.json. The generator (scripts/gen_sidecar_registry.py) merges this over registry.json; every entry needs a reason. The server evaluates every env/file rule in registry.json (credential scan, Token Health, inventory, provider list), so anything the sidecar alone should do lives here, not there. `notes` are comments carried into the generated block (JSON can't hold them), matched to a rule by `match`; `paths_contain` is a substring of one of its paths.

drop_rules.reason: Server-env session token. The sidecar reads the browser's sessionKey cookie instead and does not read this variable.
Server-env session token. The sidecar reads the browser session cookies instead and does not read this variable.
A rule type the sidecar does not implement (it would silently skip it); the server reads it from the quota snapshot instead.

add_rules.reason: The sidecar reads the CLI's OAuth token file. Not in registry.json because the server would then scan it on its own host and register a server credential for it.

github.set_reason: The sidecar's name is the service_name on its cards, which the server keys series on; registry.json says 'GitHub API' for the provider list.

drop_mapping_keys.reason: gh's `user` is a login, not the account's canonical id. Mapping it to account_id recreated the dual-account split fixed in #440, so the sidecar sends the token only and lets the server identify it.

add_rules.reason: gh >= 2.40 keeps its token in the OS keyring, so hosts.yml has no oauth_token; `gh auth token` is the only way to read it. Sidecar-only: the server never runs local commands.

drop_rules.reason: Runway's own GitHub OAuth token file. The server encrypts it at rest and reads it itself, and a sidecar can't decrypt it, so it must not be shipped from here.

add_rules.reason: Legacy kimi-cli token files the server has no reason to scan.
Attribution headers read from the sidecar's environment; not credentials the server needs.
Attribution headers read from the sidecar's environment; not credentials the server needs.

hermes.reason: Hermes Agent has no credential; the sidecar only collects its usage from local files, and the server must not list it as a provider.

notes.note: The opencode CLI stores a per-provider key in ~/.local/share/opencode/auth.json under the `openrouter.key` field. Pulling from there means a host with the opencode CLI installed lights up automatically, with no env-var setup.

The opencode CLI stores the BYOK DeepSeek key in ~/.local/share/opencode/auth.json under `deepseek.key`. The origin is fingerprinted like the other siblings, and the card still needs an account hint (Untagged Credentials) before it attaches to a labeled account.
The opencode CLI keeps its kimi-style plan keys under provider-specific names; the opencode "coding plan" variant is exposed as `minimax-coding-plan.key`.

id_token: the Google account email lives inside this JWT, not as a top-level field. Ship it so the server can derive the canonical (email) account_id instead of falling back to "default". expiry_date (ms epoch): opaque ya29.* tokens carry no JWT exp, so this is the freshness signal that stops a stale local token from clobbering a server-refreshed one.
NextAuth.js splits the session token into .0 / .1 chunks when it exceeds the 4 KB cookie size limit. Collect both so the server can reassemble them before the /api/auth/session exchange.
OpenAI service-credential cookie, required by the /api/auth/session token-exchange endpoint alongside the session token.
The opencode CLI also stores a Kimi Coding API key in auth.json under `kimi-code-plan-global.key`. Pick it up alongside the env-var rule so hosts with the opencode CLI don't need extra setup.

Kimi Code CLI OAuth credential: the access token is read-only (never the refresh token) and the server checks expires_at freshness. kimi-cli writes a per-install env file (kimi-code-env-<hash>.json), so the rule globs the credentials dir; the freshest match wins.

Ship the OAuth token so multi-host servers can call the Code Assist cloud API without accessing the local file. token.expiry is a raw ISO8601 string, converted to expiry_date (ms epoch) at collection time so the server's token_cache can compare freshness.

Primary: the opencode CLI stores the ollama-cloud API key in ~/.local/share/opencode/auth.json["ollama-cloud"].key. The collector uses it as `Authorization: Bearer ...` against https://ollama.com/api/usage for monthly quota.
